title: Why Edge AI-Driven Personalization Is The Key To Customer Loyalty
text:
Retailers are recognizing that once-cost-effective mass marketing and mass production no longer suit today’s environment, and wasted efforts can end up consuming the budget. Capri Holdings, owner of prestigious brands like Versace, Michael Kors, and Jimmy Choo, allocated over $320 million to marketing and advertising efforts in 2022, and in 2023, retail giant Walmart invested $4.4 billion. Where is this money going? Forward-thinking players must look for ways to provide personalization at scale—without compromising speed, security, or their pockets.
Traditional AI for personalization relies on sending customer data to central servers for analysis. This can be slow, inefficient, and raise privacy concerns. Edge computing brings processing power closer to the data source, directly on users’ devices or local servers, enabling organizations to make informed decisions with pace and agility.
“Its low latency makes real-time processing possible, enabling immediate and contextually relevant responses to user or sensory behavior and preferences. For example, in-store cameras powered by edge AI can continuously monitor shelves to detect low inventory levels or misplaced items, automatically triggering restocking alerts to ensure optimal product availability. Additionally, an edge AI-enabled app on a smartphone can leverage geolocation, buying patterns, and personal profile attributes to deliver targeted promotions. More importantly, it can analyze customer behavior in real-time, providing actionable insights to encourage customers to complete their transactions,” added Imtiaz Mohammady Nisum’s CEO .
By prioritizing customers and their needs — like ensuring shelves are always stocked and providing personalized promotions — customers feel valued, and their shopping experience is more convenient, driving customer loyalty.
How can edge AI be used to mitigate customer churn?
According to McKinsey, three out of four members of top-performing loyalty programs changed their behavior to generate more value for businesses: Some were purchasing more frequently, while others showed a loftier willingness to pay premiums and a higher likelihood of recommending the brand. How can AI enhance this crucial retail function?
“Just like how Spotify presents users with personalized playlists based on their listening habits in a fun way, AI at the edge can help businesses offer similar experiences — looking at in-store behavior, purchase history, and online interactions.
Say a customer just entered an Ashley Home store. Edge AI sensors and cameras start monitoring their movements and interactions, noticing that they spend a significant amount of time in the home decor section, specifically looking at modern furniture. The edge AI system, integrating this real-time data with their previous online searches and purchase history, identifies a pattern of interest in minimalist furniture.
As the customer moves through the store, digital displays and their smartphone app begin to show curated recommendations for modern furniture pieces that complement their existing preferences. They might receive notifications about new minimalistic arrivals, or promotions on items they’ve looked at but haven’t purchased yet. To make the experience more engaging, the app could also show a fun summary of their shopping habits and preferences, similar to Spotify Wrapped, highlighting their most viewed categories or frequently searched items,” Mohammady continues.
By leveraging edge AI to playfully present customer data, stores create beneficial, interactive services, and shopping becomes enjoyable and efficient. Customers feel understood, increasing their satisfaction and loyalty to the store, and personalized recommendations and timely interventions help in converting interest into purchases.
Loyalty programs often use metrics like purchase frequency and total spending to track behavior and reward customers. However, AI models can analyze a broader range of data points in real time, such as app usage frequency, on-page duration, search history, price sensitivity, product reviews, and social media interactions. This allows for a deeper understanding of customers' interests and current sentiments.
Moreover, real-time edge AI-powered analytics can play a crucial role in helping retailers manage and rectify potentially problematic situations before they escalate. For example, imagine walking into a Publix store, hovering in a specific aisle for a good while, but leaving without making a purchase. Edge AI detects this behavior and analyzes it alongside your purchase history and reviews. The system identifies a potential dissatisfaction with product availability. Immediately, a store associate is alerted to assist you.
By continuously analyzing a wide array of data points at the edge, tailored intervention can be provided in real time.
What are the ethical considerations for using edge AI in loyalty programs?
“We need to be mindful of ethics, especially when it comes to privacy. Companies owe their customers a duty of care to protect their data from breaches and unauthorized access. Therefore, data security fundamentals include encryption, access control, vulnerability management, and security awareness training.” Mohammady stresses. He notes how sector-based training, apprenticeships, upskilling, and reskilling will help businesses ensure they have the proper governance and security practices in place.
The explosion of smart devices creates a risk of constant surveillance. Facial recognition, for example—which uses AI directly on user devices without needing internet access—while useful for security, can be intrusive. According to a recent Prosper Insights & Analytics survey, 34.9% of Boomers are extremely concerned about privacy being violated from AI using our data.
“Alongside informing teams and customers of data security best practices and usage requirements, the AI itself must also be explainable. AI can inherit biases from the data it's trained on. This can lead to unfair reward distribution, favoring specific demographics over others. We need transparent and unbiased AI systems to build trust and avoid harming anyone,” Mohammady explains.
As such, businesses must use diverse datasets when training AI models for loyalty programs. This can involve partnering with data providers specializing in collecting data representative of the target customer base. Companies can also employ training techniques designed to mitigate AI model bias, such as fairness-aware regularization, to warrant app suitability across different subgroups.
What is the future of edge AI-powered customer loyalty?
A 2024 Deloitte Digital report found that over eight in ten brands predicted they'll offer personalized rewards through their loyalty programs, driven by 73% of customers demanding them.
The implementation of edge AI in loyalty programs will take various forms. For instance, voice or facial recognition AI could detect emotional cues and adjust recommendations or rewards accordingly. If a customer is frustrated, the AI could provide hyper-personalized experiences tailored to the immediate context, such as offering a targeted discount.
Another approach is incorporating AI-powered gamification and interactive experiences using augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) to enhance engagement in loyalty programs. Edge AI can analyze customer behavior on their devices in real time, enabling instant rewards. According to a recent Prosper Insights & Analytics survey, 51.6% of individuals over the age of 18 in the US participate in customer loyalty programs.
In fact, according to the survey from Prosper Insights & Analytics, 19.2% of those individuals participate in more than 5 loyalty programs.
The future of edge AI-powered customer loyalty is set to transform how businesses interact with their customers. By leveraging real-time data processing, hyper-personalization, and seamless omnichannel experiences, retailers will be able to create loyalty programs that are more engaging, secure, and effective. As technology continues to advance, the integration of edge AI with IoT devices, AR/VR, and predictive analytics will further enhance the customer experience, driving long-term loyalty and business success.

title: Community Colleges Band Together On AI Education
text:
In recent years, community and technical colleges have emerged as an underappreciated destination for AI education, stepping up to meet employer needs.
AI educational offerings exist at community colleges in most U.S. states. They range from non-credit and credit-bearing certificates to associate’s degrees and, most recently, applied bachelor’s degrees; nearly half of U.S. states permit their community colleges to offer applied baccalaureates.
Unfortunately, community colleges often face underinvestment compared to their university counterparts, and many need to build their capacity to teach effectively in emerging technology fields, which are subject to more uncertainty than established occupations. A national consortium formed by and for community colleges is set to meet that need for the AI workforce.
With a $2.8 million U.S. National Science Foundation grant, Miami Dade College, in partnership with Houston Community College and Maricopa County Community College District, is launching the National Applied Artificial Intelligence Consortium. The consortium will work to scale the access and improve the quality of AI and workforce training at community colleges.
The three institutions were early leaders in creating AI offerings at the community college level. Miami Dade, Houston, and Chandler-Gilbert Community College, a part of the Maricopa Community College District, were among the first colleges in the nation to be approved to offer applied baccalaureates in AI. The colleges will work together to promote best practices and address shared challenges with colleges nationwide.
Miami Dade President Madeline Pumariega, who has written about the college’s approach to AI education, said she was “proud” of Miami Dade College’s role as a national leader in AI workforce development and that the college was “honored to be entrusted with this important initiative.”
The consortium will be administered by faculty and staff from the three institutions co-led by Eduardo Salcedo, Lead AI faculty, and Antonio Delgado, Vice President for Technology Partnerships at Miami Dade College. Over the next three years, the consortium will help accomplish three overarching objectives:
- Improve employer partnerships: Help participating colleges improve employer advisory committees through the Business & Industry Leadership Team (BILT) model, a recognized best practice that puts colleges and employers as co-creators of curricula. The consortia will leverage BIL to collectively identify, update, and disseminate the knowledge and skill needs of college graduates to be AI workforce-ready.
- Focus on ethical AI education: Support community colleges in developing technician-level AI courses and credentials that emphasize ethics and responsible use of AI, including creating a repository of applied AI courses and resources sourced across NSF Advanced Technology Education centers and other national organizations.
- Upskill faculty: Support colleges with professional development for faculty to teach AI. The consortium will hire experts from industry and faculty from established colleges to serve as mentors to community colleges new to AI education. Each mentor will provide college support for one academic year.
The consortium has enlisted the support of several industry partners, including Intel, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, Dell, IBM, and NVIDIA. In the last few years, many of these tech companies, including Intel and Amazon, have provided funding, partnership opportunities, and technical assistance to help community colleges create these programs.
The consortium aims to leverage industry resources while ensuring that colleges are well-positioned to meet the needs of small and medium-sized employers. “This balance of large, medium and small companies will create strong pathways to employment for the students that will graduate from our AI programs," Delgado told me in an email statement.
Employer advocacy and research alike have affirmed the need for community college AI education, but more work is needed to ensure these programs are quality and lead to gainful employment. Not all jobs stemming from AI are good jobs.
Earlier this year, New America, a non-partisan policy think-tank where the author works, published the first-ever series of interviews of community college students in AI programs, which provided important lessons for AI educators and policymakers, including the value of work-based learning and community college baccalaureates.
Led by and designed for community colleges, the National Applied Artificial Intelligence Consortium is the latest national resource available to foster an AI-ready skilled technical workforce. The consortium's website invites community colleges interested in AI capacity building to join its newsletter to receive updates on opportunities to engage with activities expected to launch on October 1, 2024.

title: Is The Era Of Fairer AI Finally Here?
text:
The intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) and financial services is a hot topic. The potential for AI to revolutionize the financial services industry is immense, and it is being reflected in an endless parade of fundraise announcements, but all this AI buzz also raises important questions about the fairness, ethics, and the regulation of using AI in the provision of core financial services.
In a recent episode of "The Pnyx," we interviewed Kareem Saleh, CEO and Founder of FairPlay AI, where he delved into these issues, sharing insights on how his company is leveraging AI to create fairer lending practices. Kareem’s unique perspective, shaped by his background in both law and finance, offers a compelling look at the challenges and opportunities in this rapidly evolving field.
Here are the three main takeaways from the conversation:
1. Innovative Uses of AI Can Drive Fairer Lending
Kareem makes the case for leveraging AI for fairer lending. He shares his “ eureka moment” when he discovered that by applying adversarial debiasing techniques to a major mortgage originator's credit model, approval rates increased for Black consumers by about 10% without additional risk. By reducing reliance on conventional credit scores and optimizing the influence of other predictive variables, the mortgage originator was able to grant many billions of dollars in additional credit. This breakthrough not only facilitated 50,000 more Black families in securing homes but also demonstrated that fairer lending practices can align with financial institutions' profitability goals. Others have certainly taken notice. Last month, AI-startup Stratyfy partnered with cash flow and underwriting platform Prism Data “to help lenders make more informed decisions in cases where traditional credit data is insufficient.” Clearly, there are real opportunities for AI to democratize credit and expand lenders’ books.
2. We Must Address Disparities in Credit Underwriting
Disparities in decisioning systems often stem from “limitations in data and mathematics” rather than “people of bad faith building those models,” according to Kareem. To combat this, companies need to fine-tune the weights of various predictive variables to enhance fairness without compromising accuracy. For example, while traditional credit scores can dominate underwriting decisions, they may inadvertently perpetuate historical biases. By rebalancing the significance of these scores and integrating alternative data points, more equitable outcomes can be created for underserved communities, ensuring that deserving individuals aren't unfairly denied credit opportunities. As an industry, the solution is to be proactive; we can’t let the limited data and mathematics have their way. Investors, in particular, need to diligence AI models, as Accion details more here, prior to pouring capital fuel on the fire.
3. Balancing Innovation and Regulation is Vital
Regulation in AI is a double-edged sword and represents “one of the toughest questions” according to Kareem; over-regulation can stifle innovation and entrench the dominance of big tech companies. To ensure successful progress in AI, society must adopt smart, adaptive regulations that prevent misuse without hindering competition. Drawing parallels with the nuclear power industry's stringent regulations, Kareem argues for a balanced approach that fosters innovation while implementing safeguards to prevent ethical breaches and harmful practices. The CFPB is already taking steps in regulating AI, such as with home appraisals earlier this summer. Whether making use of other industries' frameworks or drafting something entirely new, it is paramount that regulators balance the risks alongside the benefits of AI technologies.
Conclusion
AI boasts substantial transformative potential in financial services and beyond, while also demanding careful consideration of ethical and regulatory challenges. FairPlay AI's innovative approach and vision offer an example of how we might ensure that AI-driven decisions are fair and equitable, benefiting both individuals and society as a whole. If companies implement AI correctly and ethically, it may just lead to the “strong competitive advantage” that Ganesh Rengaswamy (Managing Partner at Quona Capital) shared in our previous reflections on 2023.
The responsibility of ensuring AI is a beneficial force in society does not fall on fintech startups alone, rather all of us. Where do you see AI making significant improvements in financial services? What risks do you worry about? Let us know in the comments.

title: How Victoria’s Secret Billionaire Owner Accidentally Scored A $800 Million Stake In An AI Unicorn
text:
Les Wexner, the Victoria’s Secret billionaire who stepped down from his company L Brands in 2020 amid scrutiny over his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, is cashing in on the AI surge.
Thanks to a $1 million seed investment in Atlantic Crypto, a little-known company that would become AI cloud juggernaut CoreWeave, the 86-year-old’s family trust now holds a $720 million stake in one of the most valuable AI startups around. The Ohio-based billionaire is one of America’s wealthiest people, worth an estimated $6.3 billion.
Wexner’s massive stake in the $19 billion startup was revealed in a lawsuit filed in the United States District Court in the Southern District of New York in May 2024 by wealth management firm Florence Capital Advisors. The New York-based money manager claims it was entitled to a $6.9 million fee for advising Wexner’s family trust to invest in the startup in 2019.
CoreWeave, which provides access to highly coveted chips used in building AI models, is among the most valued AI startups to emerge from the mainstreaming of artificial intelligence. It raised $7.5 billion in debt from Blackstone in May, and $1.1 billion in equity earlier this year to build out a massive data center network that delivers the computing power needed to train AI. But back in 2019 it was a struggling cryptocurrency miner that had just started subletting its graphic chips to AI startups from a New Jersey garage.
CoreWeave raised $1.2 million in a seed round in March 2019, according to Pitchbook data. Wexner’s money manager Greg Hersch of Florence Capital invested $1 million then, later picking up another $600,000 in stock from the company’s Series A round and doubling down again through an additional convertible note. All of this was placed in a trust established for the benefit of Wexner’s four children: Sarah, Hannah, David and Harry.
Now, those investments have evolved into a $720 million stake in the AI startup that’s rumored to be seeking an initial public offering next year — and a legal squabble over what appears to be an accidental jackpot.
The spat is a rat’s nest of New York finance backstabbing involving a father-son duo brought in to manage Wexner’s money after Jeffrey Epstein allegedly stole $46 million from his family trusts, a separate $100 million stake in CoreWeave made by a bankrupt hedge fund, allegations of double-dipping and the mysterious disappearance of files containing records on the billionaire’s finances.
Florence Capital denies all this and insists it is owed a fee for an investment advice that generated “an almost unimaginable 30,986% return” when Wexner sold $71 million of CoreWeave stock in November 2023. That sale, combined with Wexner’s estimated remaining stake in CoreWeave, makes the total windfall from the investment just under $800 million.
Wexner, Florence Capital and CoreWeave did not respond to a request for comment.
Wexner’s CoreWeave investment coincided with a bet on data centers that increasingly undergird the AI wave. Since 2019, he’s sold over $450 million of land around his home in New Albany, Ohio, and in neighboring Licking County, to tech giants like Google, Meta and Facebook, and Wall Street powerhouses like Blackstone, that have used it to build massive data centers. With more than $15 billion in planned data center investments announced for Franklin and Licking Counties in the past year alone, according to the Washington D.C.-based corporate subsidy tracking watchdog Good Jobs First, Wexner is well positioned for similar deals in the future. Through his real estate development firm, the New Albany Company, he still owns some $850 million worth of farmland in the area, according to Forbes’ estimates.
A Forbes investigation published in April outlined Wexner’s crucial behind-the-scenes role in bringing a $20 billion Intel chip manufacturing factory to New Albany. The Columbus, Ohio, suburb was able to clinch the deal with Intel in a competition with dozens of other states because the New Albany Company parceled together a 1,000 “shovel-ready” block of farmland for what Intel hopes will be the world’s largest semiconductor plant. The billionaire made an estimated $35 million profit on this deal alone. He’s in the process of building a 400-acre mixed-use development adjacent to the Intel site to house its suppliers, and was still actively buying up more land as recently as July 25.

text:

title: Forget The New iPhone 16, Apple Has Something Much Better
text:
Updated August 6 with details on ChatGPT’s delayed arrival to Apple Intelligence.
Apple will launch the new iPhone 16 early in September, but a new iPhone is coming that is far more exciting for consumers than the vanilla iPhone 16. How long will you have to wait for this fourth-generation iPhone SE, and will it be worth the wait?
The current iPhone SE was launched in 2022, and the previous model in 2020. Many in the Apple community were hoping for another two-year gap and the release of an iPhone SE in 2024, but this has not come to pass. While Apple has not confirmed any SE plans, the sheer volume of leaks and data from the supply and manufacturing channels all point to a new SE being prepared for launch.
Unlike the mainline iPhones, which see annual announcements on the second Tuesday of September, there is not a tight correlation on the exact day of previous iPhone SE release dates. The original SE was launched on March 21 2017, the second generation on April 15 2020, and the third generation on March 8 2022.
Apple has traditionally launched a wave of products between mid-March and mid-April each year. Sometimes, these are the aforementioned iPhone SE models, but the late Q1 window has also been used to launch new iPads, MacBooks and Macs. While there are no pointers to the exact date for the launch of the presumptively named iPhone SE 4, you shouldn’t be too far out if you go with a late-March reveal.
One of the biggest impacts of the release date will be Apple Intelligence. While Tim Cook and his team will make a limited subset of its generative AI software available in September and allow the marketing of the iPhone 16 and iPhone 16 Pro to include AI, presumably "in a way that only Apple can", the generally accepted suite of “this is generative AI for smartphone” not arrive until Q1 2025, a date that lines up nicely with the launch of the iPhone SE.
Update: Sunday August 4: New details published this weekend highlight the trouble path the iPhone 16 is on, and why waiting for Apple to address several issues is the practical choice, even if there wasn’t a cheaper and more capable iphone SE waiting in the wings.
Writing for the Power On newsletter, Mark Gurman confirms the late arrival of Apple Intelligence. It is earmarked for iOS 18.1, which will not be available until the first half of October. With the new iPhone 16 family expected to launch on Tuesday September 10th (with retail availability from Friday September 20) they will launch without Apple Intelligence. With Google’s Pixel 9 family launching later this month and debuting Android’s second generation of generative AI, the iPhone will fall further behind 2024’s most sought-after feature.
And even when iOS 18.1 comes along it will be an incomplete AI suite. The latest beta of iOS 18 does feature this initial subset of data, and it’s not particularly special or groundbreaking, as Gurman points out:
"After testing the first beta version of Apple Intelligence, I can tell you that the features don’t yet live up to the excitement. In their current state, they’re a far cry from the game-changing technology that fans and investors hope Apple Intelligence will become."
It may not meet the expectations of those following the growth of generative AI, but it will allow Apple to marketing the iPhone as “coming with AI."
Update: Tuesday August 6: One of the biggest identifiable brands in generative AI is ChatGPT and it will be coming to Apple Intelligence. But like many of the features that consumers expect in an AI-smartphone, ChatGPT will be delivered long after Apple makes its pitch to the public that "iPhone will offer AI in a way that only Apple can” in September
Speaking to investors, Apple CEO Tim Cook stated that ChatGPT will be available across the three key operating systems for 2024: iOS 18, iPadOS 18 and macOS Sequoia. He also stated that it would not be available until the end of the calendar year.
It is expected that ChatGPT answers will be available through Siri queries. Generative text and images are available through Apple’s writing tools that reach across the platform. Basic access will be available for free (and those with a premium subscription to ChatGPT will have access to the extended software suite).
Apple executives have been heavily pushing Apple Intelligence and the inclusion of generative AI in the upcoming iPhones. It is seen as the key driver of sales for the new devices. Yet the benefits of AI already available on Android handsets will not be available for months after the launch. A subset of AI tools are currently part of the iOS 18 developer beta, but these will not be available to the public until October. To that list, we can add ChatGPT in December and the full suite of tools in the first quarter of 2025.
The true picture of what Tim Cook and his team will be able to offer through Apple Intelligence will not be clear until March 2025 at the earliest. At which point, the iPhone SE is going to be available with all of the advantages over the iPhone 16, as well as offering an informed choice around AI to consumers.
It's a safe assumption that Apple will include generative AI with the iPhone SE—considering the increasing numbers of mid-range Android Phones launching with AI it would be a courageous decision not to include it. Given the demand this places on the iPhone chipset, the iPhone SE will have to launch with the latest A18 Apple Silicon to have the required hardware capability. This wouldn't be an unusual choice for the SE; the last two generations of SE have launched with the same chipset as the current vanilla iPhone (matching the iPhone 11 and iPhone 13, respectively), although you might see an A18 chip with fewer GPU cores compared to the iPhone 16 Pro).
Nevertheless, the iPhone SE may leapfrog the iPhone 16 and debut new hardware. Noted analyst Ming-Chi Kuo reports that after many years of delays and frustrations, Apple is finally reading to use its own 5G modem design in its hardware. The iPhone line currently relies on Qualcomm for a cellular connection, forcing Apple to accommodate third-party hardware. Owning the modem would mean efficiencies in iOS, which could offer faster connectivity using less battery power. Kuo also reports that the new modem could debut with the iPhone SE.
If the iPhone SE can offer a full suite of AI tools, a faster and more efficient modem, and the same powerful specs at a lower price than the iPhone 16, the launch date becomes a crucial part of the decision-making process on which iPhone to purchase. March 2025 is not that far away to get the first consumer-focused iPhone for a new generation.
Now read the latest iPhone, iPad, and Mac headlines in Forbes’ weekly Apple Loop news digest...

title: Is The AI Bubble About To Burst?
text:
Following a turbulent few weeks in the stock market, there’s a lot of speculation that the AI “bubble” may be about to burst.
Many companies that are involved in AI have seen the value of their stock rocket dramatically over the past year or so. The most celebrated example is Nvidia, whose stock price has more than tripled over the past year. Others heavily invested in AI, such as Google and Microsoft, have also seen large increases.
Big leaps in stock price – particularly when they seem difficult to link to the generation of real value – are sometimes seen by analysts as an indicator that prices are due for a correction.
It’s hard to shake the feeling that we’ve seen all of this before. The peak of hype and excitement around the newly-emerged internet, around the year 2000, was swiftly followed by the bursting of the "dot com bubble." Many companies went out of business, the economy experienced a significant downturn, and many jobs were lost.
So, is this a bubble? While it is said that AI could add around $15 trillion to the value of the global economy, recent earnings reports from the likes of Google and Tesla have been less than stellar, leading to the recent dips in share prices. At the same time, there are reports that the general public is becoming more distrustful of AI and that businesses are finding it difficult to make money from it.
Does this mean that the AI revolution – touted as holding the solution to problems as diverse as curing cancer and saving the environment – is about to come crashing down around our ears?
Personally, I don’t think so. But even if it does, in the long run, that might not even turn out to be a bad thing for AI adoption.
Is This 2000 All Over Again?
There are certainly striking similarities between what we are seeing today and the economic and market conditions that led up to the great dot com bubble burst of 2000.
During both periods, we’ve seen huge increases in stock prices and company valuations, seemingly driven by hopes and expectations for the future rather than tangible present-day results.
This has led to big stock indexes like the S&P 500, which heavily consists of tech stocks, mirroring the weighting of internet companies back at the turn of the century.
Just as was the case with the internet back then, all large companies are seeking to increase their valuations by leveraging their commitment to AI, with its promise of unlocking huge profits and growth further down the road.
However, there are also some very important differences. For a start, today’s AI leaders – companies like Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet and Meta – are already hugely profitable. They have proven business models and solid, reliable revenue streams that most likely won’t dry up even in the unlikely scenario that all of their AI plans fail.
This simply wasn’t the case for many of the hundreds of companies that failed when the dot com bubble burst – most of which you’ve probably completely forgotten about by now.
With “all their eggs in one basket,” so to speak, they were just not set up to survive even a temporary dip in the market’s enthusiasm for the internet gold rush.
Things are very different today. Even if it turns out we’re not quite ready to make the leap to a fully automated, AI-driven society just yet, Google and Meta’s advertising services, Amazon’s shopping business and Tesla’s cars will keep those companies going until we are.
In addition, their huge user bases and vast amounts of proprietary data serve as protection against upstarts hoping to sneak in and launch competing AI services under their noses.
So It’s Safe For Me To Invest All My Money In AI Stocks, Then?
Okay, well, first of all, of course, nothing I say here should be taken as investment advice as I am not a financial advisor by any means.
But here’s my opinion. It's clear that the hugely inflated valuations we've seen in the past year or two are indicative of a bubble; a correction could very well be on the cards and may even be underway right now.
Despite this, however, I believe the mid and long-term prospects for AI are incredibly strong. It certainly has the potential to be just as – if not more – transformative than the emergence of the internet in the late 20th century eventually proved to be.
I also believe that part of the reason we haven’t seen many companies achieving real tangible value with AI just yet is that many leaders still aren't prepared for the AI revolution. You can read more about my thoughts about that here.
As the dot com bubble burst, companies that didn’t survive were those that failed to think strategically about how the internet would impact their business and the opportunities it created.
Meanwhile, those that approached the internet not just as an opportunity to bring an existing business model online but as a way to radically rethink it from the ground up – Amazon, Google, and Netflix are just three of the most obvious examples – not only recovered but reached even greater heights.
This is why, even for a firm believer in the potential of AI like myself, acknowledging the likelihood we are in a bubble of some sort and the fact that there could be some turbulence ahead is important.
Market corrections serve to remind us that the true, transformative potential of revolutionary advances like AI (or indeed the internet) lies in their practical applications and the real value they create rather than in speculative excitement and hype.
By refocusing our attention on genuine innovation and its tangible benefits, we become better equipped to recognize this value and make more informed decisions about our investments in the future of AI.

title: Harnessing Generative AI For Sustainable Food Systems Innovation
text:
Generative AI, a type of Artificial Intelligence that involves creating new content or solutions, based on the generation of new data, scenarios, and models, is emerging as a game-changer in driving innovation, with significant social and environmental potential at the food-health-climate nexus.
Novel insights, driven by analyses of vast amounts of data, based on broad stakeholder engagement, can transform how food companies innovate. These insights have the power to optimize productivity, accelerate sustainability, and enhance human health, ensuring that food production meets the needs of both consumers and producers without compromising planetary health.
According to a recent survey by the Capgemini Research Institute, around 40% of food and beverage companies are currently utilizing AI, with many also exploring generative AI.
To improve global food security and sustainability, innovation is essential, and generative AI has the capability to enhance inclusivity within the innovation process.
Power dynamics in the food sector place significant control in the hands of a few key players who influence decisions regarding what food is grown, where and when it is produced, and how it is processed, distributed, and consumed. Sustainable development demands more diverse perspectives in decision-making.
"Critical tech decisions in healthcare, climate, and food have been monopolized by a narrow clique of privileged voices for far too long," affirms Yasmin Shmuel, CEO and Co-Founder of KLEVER AI, an AI and machine learning platform featuring "decision rooms" that harness “collective decision intelligence,” to unlock valuable insights, drive operational efficiency, and make data-driven decisions with confidence.
KLEVER AI’s decision-making technology has applications across various industries, with significant potential for health and food and beverage. Considering that food systems account for a third of global anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions and consume 70% of the world’s freshwater resources, leveraging generative AI in this sector could drive substantial positive global change.
The first UN Food Systems Summit (UNFSS), held in September 2021, made it clear that the transformation of food systems requires the active participation and inclusion of all stakeholders. This approach not only ensures that diverse perspectives and knowledge are leveraged but also promotes equity, innovation, and resilience.
“The long-term public benefits food systems must deliver and challenge the short-term individual interests that currently distort our food systems,” said African Food Fellowship Director Joost Guijt, in support of the summit’s objectives.
Shmuel believes that Klever AI’s approach to generative AI is a catalyst for change in such industries, which have long been dominated by what she refers to as “homogeneous thinking.” She emphasizes the staggering 70% failure rate in tech adoption as evidence of a system that is not working.
“Lives hang in the balance, yet we're still allowing the same insular group of decision-makers to dictate our future," she says. “Diversity of thought unlocks boundless potential.
Data-driven food systems can revolutionize production, distribution, and consumption. By leveraging generative AI throughout the supply chain, companies can enhance sustainability, optimize operations, improve sourcing, and adopt circular economy practices.
In the realm of food sustainability and precision agriculture, generative AI can analyze complex datasets to recommend practices that reduce environmental impact while enhancing productivity. For example, AI can optimize crop rotations and resource use, ensuring sustainable agricultural practices that align with environmental goals.
“For agriculture, it’s coming at us in ways that make it easier for producers to do their job, and do it better,” said Nina Schick, founder of Tamang Ventures, in her keynote at evokeAG. 2024.
According to data from AI4D Africa, despite representing just 2.5% of the global AI market, emerging applications could boost Africa's economic growth by $2.9 trillion by 2030. Currently, about half of AI on the continent has agricultural applications.
In 2023, Viamo launched Ask Viamo Anything— a generative AI voice assistant— on its platforms in Zambia and Nigeria, providing free, crucial information via feature phones without internet access. This service was particularly beneficial for those with low literacy and marginalized groups like women and persons with disabilities. Pilot results indicated women asked 50% more questions than men in Zambia and 30% more in Nigeria. The platform has 1.35 million users in Nigeria alone.
Generative AI also has a pivotal role in addressing health-related aspects of food production.
Given that nine of the top fifteen global risk factors for morbidity, such as high body mass index (BMI), high blood pressure, cardiac disease, diabetes, and malnutrition, are linked to poor diet, the transformative implications are vast.
By analyzing nutritional data, consumer behavior, and health outcomes, AI can help design food products that promote better health. This synergy between food and health technology can lead to the development of functional foods that address specific health issues, such as diabetes or heart disease, thus contributing to overall public health.
At IFT FIRST, the annual event of the Institute of Food Technologists which took place in July, Nora Khaldi, CEO of Nuritas, a Biotechnology company in Dublin, Ireland, showed how generative AI was being used to optimize food production to promote better health for consumers.
Khaldi explained that Nuritas is using generative AI to determine the “types of ingredients that the industry likes [and] how can we create something that’s better, but like it.”
One example is Nuritas’ development of an ingredient called PeptiStrong, to enhance muscle health.
“It’s an ingredient that would have taken 30 million years to discover through traditional ways,” she explained. “Through AI we can shorten that down to two years.”
Notco, a food-tech company, employs AI to create plant-based substitutes for animal products, while Nutrino utilizes AI algorithms to provide personalized dietary recommendations, helping individuals make informed food choices for a healthier lifestyle.
Generative AI has also supported product development for flavor, seasonings and spices manufacturer, McCormick & Company.
McCormick’s proprietary generative AI-powered product platform, "ONE," uses insights extracted from datasets on consumer preferences and market trends to develop new products, featuring unique flavor combinations that meet its customers’ changing tastes.
From a supply chain perspective, generative AI has the potential to enhance innovation, profitability, and sustainability from farm to fork by improving forecasting, traceability, safety, and waste reduction.
According to a study conducted by Bain, some 68% of executives believe that digital traceability is essential, and with a third of all food produced globally going to waste, AI helps ensure that food is produced and distributed more efficiently, minimizing surplus and spoilage.
Walmart is using generative AI to optimize its supply chain, forecasting product demand, enhancing its ability to manage inventory and streamline shipment tracking.
Generative AI facilitates vertical integration by breaking down silos, allowing companies to seamlessly coordinate and optimize processes across different stages of production and distribution, with opportunities for inclusivity, and enhanced sustainability.
According to the R&D director of a large healthcare enterprise that leveraged technology from KLEVER AI, the medical industry “has been glacially slow to adapt,” and KLEVER’s generative AI platform “is forcing us to confront the fact that our siloed approach has been stunting our growth.”
Both producers and consumers have an equally critical role to play in creating change, but processes must be implemented to allow voices on both sides to be heard.
“The overworked nurse, the skeptical climate scientist, the food safety advocate fighting for stringent regulations— these aren't just token voices; they're the backbone of innovation,” says Andriy Golubitskiy, Chief Technology Officer at KLEVER AI.
"We're not interested in echo chambers or yes-men," agrees Javier Sanchez, KLEVER’s VP of AI. "Our AI thrives on dissent, on the messy reality of complex industries.
By amplifying the voices of engineers—voices that have been systematically overlooked—the team at KLEVER says that it has seen decisions become six times faster and three times more effective. This approach has essentially redefined what "expertise" means in healthcare, climate, and food tech, bringing the insights of women leaders, climate scientists in the field, and food safety experts on the front lines into the fold.
“These are the people intimately familiar with the tech that impacts our lives every day. Their perspectives aren't just valuable—they're vital,” says Shmuel.
This sentiment is echoed across industries, demonstrating that the integration of diverse perspectives not only accelerates innovation but also enhances the effectiveness and sustainability of technology decisions.
As AI continues to shape the future of food and health, ethical considerations and collaborative efforts are paramount. Generative AI has the potential to create more fairness, transparency, and accountability. The inclusion of diverse voices is not just an ethical imperative but a strategic necessity to develop solutions that are innovative, equitable and sustainable.
The stakes for relying on outdated approaches to decision-making across the food system are incredibly high.
Generative AI and machine learning solutions transform and empower food businesses to thrive in the digital age, gain a competitive edge, and fulfill their social and environmental responsibilities.
"Our current decision-making processes are not good enough,” affirms Shmuel. “They're costing lives, stifling innovation, and perpetuating a system that values conformity over competence. As AI guru Andrew Ng said, 'AI will not disrupt people; people that use AI will disrupt people who do not use AI.' It's time to embrace AI as a tool for revolutionary change, not as a competitor."

title: Council Post: Generative AI Will Replace Everything: Rethinking User Experience
text:
Arran Stewart is the cofounder and CVO of Job.com. Technologist, car nut and proud father.
The title of this article may seem bold and provocative.
While I might aim to capture attention, let me clarify: I do not believe that generative AI (GenAI) will replace everything. More to the point, I don’t necessarily believe that the current iterations of generative AI like ChatGPT or Claude will be the dominant technology or user experience (UX) in the future. These technologies are currently top of mind among users and consumers, but the first technology to receive public attention and buy-in isn’t always dominant in the end—just ask Yahoo.
With this article, since generative AI is something most people can now relate to and understand, I am going to use the technology as a jumping-off point to discuss how companies should be looking to improve user experience in the coming years.
How Conversational AI And GenAI Will Impact UX
With the rise of conversational AI, the way users interact with technology has evolved immensely. Conversational AI technology already serves many of our daily needs—just ask Siri, Alexa and Google Home. These solutions can already play your favorite music or tell you the weather.
But these are still primitive applications of the technology's potential.
As generative AI evolves, it will allow conversational AI to perform more complex tasks. Consider if a solution can learn the needs and wants of the consumer—which many companies are already exploring—and fill in many of the gaps within daily processes. For example, ordering a gallon of milk. The AI could determine the best price, the best delivery time and maybe even the frequency of delivery based on the user’s consumption needs.
It would be intelligent, intuitive and proactive, and it would provide a far more streamlined experience for users. In short, it would be a digital augmentation of the human being in a way we have never seen before.
Today, companies spend a considerable amount of time and money to create seamless experiences within their user experience and user interface (UI). What could be coming is a greatly reduced need for that level of engagement and interaction if something like generative AI could layer over it in the ways described above.
Let's look at some potential real-world examples.
Buying Groceries
The latest and greatest grocery shopping experience is a digital one, using platforms like Instacart or retailers’ websites to order, purchase and often deliver groceries. This digital experience saves time compared to physically going to the grocery store and can be further streamlined with features such as saved items and automated repeat orders.
But generative AI offers the potential to add a middleware layer that makes using these platforms even more frictionless and natural. Using useful queries and natural language, this middleware could convert our vocalized instructions into action via ambient technology hardware like Siri, Alexa and Google Home.
The core technology here would be generative AI that conversationally enacts our consumption on a supply chain solution.
Instead of physically visiting the grocery delivery app on their device, users would instead interact with the platform through a layered-over interpreter known as conversational AI that acts as a digital concierge carrying out the tasks.
Applying For A Job
As an expert in the HR technology space, I can attest that the job search process—and, specifically, the job application process—requires many moving parts: search engines, job boards, applicant tracking systems, résumé uploads, AI matching and more.
The application tracking system (ATS) will always remain part of the process for compliance and distribution, and it is necessary as a system of record for companies, particularly for hiring records required by the IRS.
However, layering generative AI over an ATS or job listing platform could act as an information aggregator. Although it may call for significant configuration to meet compliance and data requirements, it could enable smart applications, identifying potential job fit and executing a job application.
Conversational AI has the potential to provide information to the user such as job details, job matches and company insights. It would be very useful to have this solution as a preemptive guide for predicting the likelihood of success and candidate-job match before a candidate even applies.
Conclusion
So, what will push the digital world to work in such a way? Well, it’s already being pushed this way with the rise of domestic ambient technologies such as Alexa and Google Home. Most of us already have told Siri "No" or "Not right now" as it abruptly interrupts us during our day.
As more users engage with ambient technology applications, both hardware and software, it will put increasing pressure on brands to rethink their digital experiences to accommodate how their customers interact with them.
This type of technology is still not here—and there are, of course, many barriers. For example, who pays for this technology? Do companies implement it themselves, or would a third party act as a middleman?
But brands should start thinking differently about UX now. As users become more and more used to conversational AI technology, they will engage with companies and technology in new and different ways.
For example, what does the user experience of rideshare companies look like when happens when users say, "I need a ride," and generative AI automatically calls the cheapest option between Uber, Lyft and other cab services? How does this impact the rideshare business model? It would certainly impact the loyalty that Uber and Lyft have created over the years, but it is also the next logical progression from what Booking.com brought to the hotels or what Opentable has done for restaurants, right?
All I can conclude is that we are at the beginning of the process, as Siri, Alexa and generative AI are paving the way. We must ask ourselves now: What will those technologies become smart enough in the future to do?

title: This Startup Raised $25 Million To Keep Data Safe While Training AI
text:
The rise of generative AI models has attracted interest for a number of different applications, but both businesses and individuals increasingly rely on cloud-based services while training and deploying AI, which increases the risk of security breaches and data leaks.
Palo Alto, California-based Anjuna wants to reduce that risk using a process called confidential computing it offers in its Seaglass architecture, which creates virtual data exchange boxes that protect data while it’s being accessed. Once connected to these encrypted rooms, that data can be used for tasks such as training AI models, analyzing sensitive information or collaborating on research while reducing the threat of hacks, data breaches or leaks.
"We've essentially built what we call a universal confidential computing platform," cofounder and CEO Ayal Yogev told Forbes. "We didn't invent confidential computing — we're just here to make it extremely easy."
Today, Anjuna announced it has raised $25 million in a series B2 funding led by M Ventures, SineWave Ventures and AI Capital Partners. The round brings the company's investment to date to $67 million. One major purpose for the influx of capital is for the company to further develop its new AI Clean Rooms feature, which is only available in an early version to select clients.
Born in Israel, Yogev, 44, studied electrical engineering and computer science at Tel-Aviv University before joining Unit 8200, one of Israel's most famous military intelligence and technology units. After completing an MBA at UC Berkeley, he went into enterprise security, holding multiple management positions at companies like SafeBreach, Lookout and OpenDNS and Imperva. In 2018, he founded Anjuna with Yan Michalevsky, 42, who he had known for more than 20 years and reconnected with while he was completing his doctorate degree at Stanford.
"We're almost like an operating system company,"
Confidential computing isn’t new. Chipmakers like Intel, Microsoft and ARM have embedded hardware in their CPUs and GPUs that enable the creation of these zones at the server level. But the software they built to enable these features are often not compatible with each other, making collaboration difficult. When Yogev and Michalevsky caught wind of this, they were excited to find a way to do something that hadn’t been done before: create a solution that solved the compatibility problem.
Fixing this issue is key, they realized, to enabling companies to take advantage of advanced AI models. For example, if a healthcare company wants to employ an AI company to train a model on disease detection without sharing sensitive patient data with the company, Anjuna's Clean Room allows the model to be fully trained in the virtual room. This way, although both the code and data are in the same space, each company only has access to its own information. This is challenging with conventional solutions because they often rely on less secure methods that do not fully isolate data during the collaborative process. That’s because they lack the required comprehensive encryption needed to protect data in use.
Securing the data sounds simple but it’s easier said than done: because confidential computing has conventionally been hardware-focused, building the software with the necessary encryption requires working at a deep level in the system stack. That means that Anjuna’s developers need to have more knowledge of underlying computer system infrastructure, rather than just application level programming. This adds layers of complexity to developing their platform. "We're almost like an operating system company," Yogev said.
Wayne Duso, a technology advisor at both Bedrock Security and Anjuna, told Forbes that working at this level and being compatible with multiple types of hardware is what enables Anjuna to be competitive in the market.
"What these folks have done is they have figured out a way of making the process seamless to the current developers process for developing, testing and securing deploying and executing code," he said. “They have made hard simple.”
Laura Martinez, director of security marketing at NVIDIA said that another advantage of confidential computing is that it could encourage companies to collaborate on projects they otherwise wouldn’t have without being worried about losing sensitive data.
“It already is beginning to revolutionize how businesses engage with each other especially in healthcare and financial services,” she said. “I see everything in a confidential computing environment hopefully in the near future.”
Moving forward, Yogev said that his company aims to make this environment more accessible by the end of the year, which is when the company plans to offer its features on the broader market. “We’re expanding our go-to market,” he said. “Confidential computing is going to be the next big enabler.”

title: Council Post: It's Time To Reframe How We Think About AI
text:
Roger Hurni, co-founder of Off Madison Ave, a behavioral marketing agency, & Lighthouse PE, a marketing automation software for mobile apps
Artificial intelligence is on everyone's mind. To some, it’s a bold new frontier. To others, it's a paradigm shift in how companies will function. But for most people, it's a question mark, meaning there's a general fear of it and what it will do.
Even people who want to work with AI generally don't know where to start. And if they do, they are often averse to risks such as copyright infringement, plagiarism and hallucinations.
People have always feared new technology and its implications. You can go all the way back to the printing press. I've seen it with the introductions of the Macintosh computer, the internet, digital marketing and social media. Each one has had a profound impact on the world.
Drawing on behavioral science, one of the best ways to gain acceptance of a product is to reframe it to be more easily understood or have greater appeal. Thinking about AI differently can do that for you. This is why you must reframe AI for what it really is: artificial interpretation.
Think about it. AI is not really artificial intelligence. It is not sui generis, nor is it a sentient entity. It doesn’t come up with new ideas (unless it's hallucinating).
For now, AI is simply a simulation of human intelligence that can perform tasks like learning and problem-solving. More specifically, AI finds correlations in seemingly unrelated data. Then, it uses those correlations to interpret existing information in a new way. Hence, artificial interpretation.
A Better Way To Approach AI
In my experience, it’s vital to approach AI from a human-centric perspective. This makes it much easier to apply rules to it, implement it, and have it profoundly change you and your business. This approach will also help you better connect with your customers, communicate value to them and shift their behavior.
One of the primary things I tell organizations is that if they want to shift a big behavior, they must break it down into smaller components. I’ve been teaching my teenage son to drive. I certainly didn’t expect him to get into the car for the first time and drive, even though he's had a vast amount of experience watching people drive in videos, being in cars and reading all about the rules of the road.
He could take that knowledge base and start driving if he were AI as we currently define it. But he’s not capable of actually driving, regardless of the knowledge base. And yet, that is what we expect AI to do. Most people seem to believe that AI can use that knowledge base effectively from the start, which is a mistake.
Start Small And Teach AI What You Want
To put it another way, let’s look at onboarding a new employee. Sadly, many companies don’t get employee onboarding right. They hire someone and provide that person with little to no training. Based on the new employee’s past experience, the company expects them to perform a job. It’s just like that with an AI’s collective knowledge base. You are expecting it to perform a job without training it properly.
And that is the real trick to AI: approaching it from the point of view of teaching, not receiving an answer.
But this is more than just breaking down your giant prompt into smaller prompts that teach the AI along the way. You also have to consider the human elements behind it. This means considering people's motivations, the emotional impact you want for the AI outcome, and how that outcome will affect the expectations of those audiences interacting with it. It’s a human-centric approach.
Taking A Human-Centric Approach To AI For Business
There’s a lot of news about AI being used to impersonate celebrities, politicians and voice talent. You can program an AI to mimic anybody’s voice. You can make it say things that person never said. And that could be dangerous. It can also be used for good, such as using sports announcer Al Michaels' voice (with permission) as an AI bot to provide daily recaps of the Summer Olympics.
Some brands are likely using audio AI because they want to sidestep talent payments. It works like this: You start by paying an actor to be in a studio to read the script. But later on, you might want to change that script or have an entirely different script read. Instead of hiring that actor again, you can use AI to read the script in the actor’s voice.
However, the AI voice simulation is missing the actor’s ability to draw on their past experiences, as well as the character’s motivations and the actor's interpretation of what that character might do next. This human approach brings with it a richer, more artistic performance. That can determine how loud or soft a line of copy is delivered and which words are emphasized. It can determine when pauses or an “umm” should be placed in the middle of a thought.
I’m not saying we shouldn't use AI because actors are getting the short end of the stick. That’s an entirely different subject in contract negotiations.
To maximize the effectiveness of AI, you have to consider all of the emotional states, the character's motivation and the nuances of thought. That is far more important than simply having the AI read the script in the same voice as the actual actor.
The point of all of this is to think of AI as artificial interpretation. Don't start by asking an AI to write a brand persona based on generic demographic information. It would be best if you taught the AI context. Start small, and every time you get an answer, add to the richness and complexity of your prompt. Getting to your desired answer may take half a dozen prompts, but your patience will be rewarded.

title: Council Post: Convergence Marketing: Balancing Automation With Human Relationships
text:
David Corchado, Co-Founder & Chief Strategy & Technology Officer at Avenue Z, is a leader in automation, media optimization, and e-commerce.
In a paradigm shift about to revolutionize our industry, I see us moving beyond the outdated concept of integrated marketing with its siloed approach to channel-specific messaging.
Instead, the future is convergence marketing. With the growing accessibility of large language models (LLMs), balancing platform integration with integrity is now a problem of the past. But while AI is revolutionizing content creation, it lacks a crucial element: Genuine human empathy. This isn't just feel-good fluff; it's the cornerstone of building trust and reciprocity with our audience.
Make no mistake, AI is poised to dominate the content landscape. From news broadcasts to social feeds, it's reshaping how we communicate. But human connection is our ace in the hole.
Therefore, a winning strategy lies at the intersection of AI-driven efficiency and human-centric engagement. This is the essence of convergence marketing. We're not pitting humans against machines; we're leveraging both to create something truly game-changing.
Convergence Marketing
A well-planned convergence strategy is consistent and immersive across all touchpoints. I think a great example is Nike’s Air Max Day campaign where they used engaging posts and stories on Instagram and TikTok, which featured user-generated content and influencer collaborations. As a part of the campaign, they also sent personalized emails to members with exclusive previews and early access to new releases. In-store, they held special events and promotions, and through their mobile app, they offered exclusive content and deals.
Another great example is Urban Outfitters’ “Shift Happens” back-to-school campaign. Again, they were able to combine marketing platforms and channels. As part of a social media partnership, they collaborated with Pinterest and had influencers create brand-forward boards.
A two-day event at The Chelsea Factory in New York City featured live performances and an immersive shopping experience that helped in-person activation. Following that activation, they used college pop-ups with limited-edition drops from partner brands.
These campaigns give a taste of how brands can create a seamless customer experience across channels by maintaining a consistent message, leveraging user-generated content and personalizing interactions. Marketers can overcome challenges like message coherence and platform management by focusing on a unified strategy with clear brand guidelines.
Getting Your Technology Right
Sephora is a prime example of a company that has successfully integrated AI to enhance its marketing efforts. Using AI-driven data analytics, they are able to personalize customer experiences both online and in-store. For instance, their virtual artist tool allows customers to try on makeup virtually using augmented reality (AR), delivering tailored recommendations and a seamless shopping experience.
Another example is how Carl’s Jr. leveraged AI-powered contextual targeting for connected television (CTV) advertising. Using IRIS.TV’s private marketplace, the company was able to conduct a campaign that helped drive in-store visits and sales. They demonstrated how AI can enhance advertising efforts by analyzing CTV content frame by frame and targeting specific audience segments.
Overall, AI-driven technologies like chatbots, predictive analytics and personalized marketing have proven highly effective in enhancing customer experiences. When looking into this strategy, brands can start with data analysis to help understand customer behavior and preferences. Note, though, that addressing data privacy concerns and the complexity of integrating AI systems requires transparent data policies and phased implementation strategies.
Customer Experience Management
Qatar Airways' AI-enhanced digital cabin crew member, Sama, is an intriguing example of customer service, interacting with customers in real time, providing up-to-date information and answering frequently asked questions. Integrated with OpenAI, Sama enhances the overall travel experience with accurate information.
In contrast, brands like Etsy are tackling AI anxiety among stakeholders with a new ad campaign and platform guidelines emphasizing a human touch. Etsy's initiative reassures both sellers and buyers of the platform's commitment to authenticity and craftsmanship.
To continuously improve the customer experience, brands should leverage customer feedback through surveys, social media listening and direct interactions. Balancing automation with a human element involves using data to personalize interactions while maintaining a human touch in customer service.
Content Strategy
Apple’s "Shot on iPhone" campaign leveraged user-generated content to highlight the iPhone’s camera capabilities. As a part of the marketing campaign, their social media, billboards and print ads featured photos and videos taken by users. Television and online ads highlighted the stories behind the photos and the technology that made them possible.
Some other noteworthy campaigns from 2024 include:
• CeraVe’s Super Bowl ad: Featuring Michael Cera, the campaign achieved over 32 billion earned impressions, significantly boosting sales through creative guerrilla marketing tactics combining TV ads with social media, influencer marketing and online content.
• Lay’s Groundhog Day campaign: Running eight spots 75 times on ABC on Groundhog Day, featuring Stephen Tobolowsky, the campaign achieved 1.4 billion earned media impressions by resonating with viewers through a repetitive, engaging narrative.
• Heineken’s "the boring phone" campaign: Releasing a limited-edition “dumb phone” lacking internet access, Heineken garnered over 24,000 sign-ups within an hour of launch, combining product innovation with experiential marketing and digital engagement.
Lessons from this: Brands can encourage customer participation by creating easy-to-join initiatives and offering incentives. Key metrics for evaluating multichannel content strategies include engagement rates, user-generated content volume and conversion rates. Look to analyze performance data and adjust strategies accordingly.
Balancing Automation And Human Relationships
Despite the efficiency and scalability that automation provides, it cannot replace the depth of human empathy and understanding. For example, while Sephora’s AI tools handle routine queries and offer recommendations, this frees up human employees to focus on complex customer needs and personalized interactions. This approach ensures that while technology enhances efficiency, the human touch remains central to customer service.
Bots and AI can handle repetitive tasks, but human oversight is essential for avoiding the impersonal. Personalized emails and targeted social media campaigns should always retain a level of human insight to connect with the audience.
As of today, humans are still far better at using creative storytellers than our AI counterparts. High-quality content will come to be defined as real-time AI-created content that is human-checked for desired tone, context and cultural nuance and refined to eliminate potential bias and create emotional resonance.

title: Council Post: Harnessing Generative AI: A $4.4 Trillion Opportunity For The Global Economy
text:
David Jones is Vice President, Technology Portfolio at IDA Ireland.
Generative AI could add up to $4.4 trillion to the global economy—not over a decade but annually.
The transformational change that's about to happen with AI is similar to the early days of the internet. Indeed, organizations that don't embrace AI today risk losing their market position or becoming obsolete like those that didn't take their business online more than two decades ago.
How can companies make sure they're prepared to embrace AI in an effective, scalable and ethical way?
In an April 2024 generative AI survey, Deloitte found that AI-savvy organizations are moving past what it calls the "infatuation stage." Instead, these companies are focused on fast adoption and overcoming technical and organizational barriers to generative AI. They're investing more in infrastructure and changing their talent strategies—not only to upskill employees for AI but to also hire new employees to support their AI initiatives.
As organizations strive to create and deploy AI applications to improve efficiency and productivity, here are three actions that C-suite technology leaders should consider taking as they work to make sure their global operations—and especially their global workforce—are ready.
1. Choose Strategic Global Locations With Value-Add Talent
For companies racing to adopt and adapt AI technologies, a top need is talent. The roles that companies need as they increase AI adoption include not only data scientists and machine learning engineers but also specialists like prompt engineers, AI ethicists and AI translators.
Not surprisingly, the talent pipeline isn't yet flush with people holding these unique skills. Thomson Reuters predicted that the hiring gap would be about 50% for all needed AI positions in 2024.
Now, companies are making talent a top priority as they consider how and where to launch their AI initiatives.
For example, in May 2024, IBM (a partner of ours) announced an investment in Ireland that will significantly expand its operations, adding up to 800 high-tech jobs. The positions will help build advanced software based on generative AI technologies for areas such as security, automation and hybrid cloud. IBM specifically mentioned Ireland's "caliber of talent" when announcing the investment.
Building a talent base to attract such an investment doesn't happen overnight. Ireland's presence in AI is 20 years in the making. The country has the world's first industry-driven postgraduate master's level course in AI and is home to one of Europe's largest data analytics research organizations that's doing work in AI. In Dublin alone, roughly 1 in 6 engineers now have AI experience, which is double the European Union average.
2. Be Active In Policy Conversations
As companies weigh potential locations in Europe for their AI initiatives, the new EU AI Act is top of mind. The act is significant because it's the world's first regulation in a major economy to govern AI. The act also has an extraterritorial effect, meaning it applies to anyone in the world operating an AI system in the EU or using the output of an AI system operated in the EU.
EU member states gave final approval to the act in March 2024, and it is expected to go into effect soon. The act bans certain uses of AI and places some requirements on providers of AI systems that are deemed to be "high risk." Additionally, the EU Commission will be able to fine companies $38 million or 7% of their annual revenue for breaching the act.
Some in the business world have lamented that the EU is regulating itself out of AI innovation. However, the truth is that the EU AI Act provides some commonsense guardrails that will help protect people from the misuse of AI technologies.
While the EU AI Act is on the verge of taking effect, it may just be the start of AI regulations in Europe. With EU elections being held in 2024, voters' sentiments about AI could show up at the polls and inspire further regulatory action down the road.
Companies that want their voices heard on AI regulations should share them with members of the D9+, which is where any new regulations would stem from. Some member countries like Ireland take pride in being open to conversations with industry about important matters like AI and regulations.
3. Maintain Trust
How much societies accept AI technology, and how strongly governments want to further regulate it, will be largely influenced by one factor—trust. Today, only 3 in 10 people globally embrace AI.
Companies are working to build trust in AI in several ways. For example, major global brands have joined efforts like the Partnership on AI, which seeks to use AI developments to advance positive outcomes for people and society. Many companies have also created policies and guidance to help develop and deploy AI responsibly.
Countries are also making trustworthy AI a priority. Here in Ireland, the government has worked to make the country a global leader in the use of ethical and trustworthy AI to benefit the economy and society. Companies like OpenAI have also invested in the country specifically to support their work in areas like trust and safety.
Companies are also trying to mitigate risk as they establish and grow their AI operations. They want to know they can innovate and maintain the security and privacy of data without having to worry, for instance, about wild policy swings with each election. Even seemingly minor things like countries having business-friendly governments and workforces that have shared cultural and historic ties with their home countries can reassure companies when choosing where to locate their operations.
A New Economy Ready For The Taking
AI is on the verge of reinventing work. Now is the time when companies need to implement global, talent-led strategies to create the technologies that make that reinvention possible. Those that get it right have an opportunity to claim a leading role in a new, more productive global economy.
